source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. VII (Montreuil)

1.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI PRIMI : VERBA ECCLESIASTÆ FILII DAVID REGIS JERUSALEM.
1.title_en: Elucidation of the first chapter: The words of Ecclesiastes, the son of David, king of Jerusalem.

paras.t: Quemadmodum Salomon tria sortitus sit nomina, et juxta illorum trium nominum interpretationem tria ediderit volumina, ad tres hominum status spectantia, introductum est supra, in exordio expositionis libri Proverbiorum : ideo illa non videntur hic repetenda. Itaque iste est liber secundus ac medius Salomonis. Qui liber a suo auctore Ecclesiastes, id est concionator, interpretatur : quoniam sicut concionatoris est, in personis plurium loqui, et tandem concludendo ac definiendo sententiam, quid tenendum sit, determinare, atque per hoc tumultuantis ac discrepantis inter se turbæ sedare discordiam; sic Salomon in libro isto in personis loquitur diversorum, diversa opinantium ac sentientium. Et frequenter, quid salubriter sit tenendum, definit : imo in fine voluminis, quid de necessitate salutis credi et fieri ab universis oporteat, introducit, dicendo : Finem loquendi pariter omnes audiamus : Deum time, et mandata ejus observa.
paras.en: How Solomon received three names, and, according to the meaning of those three names, put forth three volumes, which concern three states of men, was set out above, at the beginning of the exposition of the book of Proverbs; so it does not seem that it need be repeated here. This, then, is the second and middle book of Solomon. This book is named by its author Ecclesiastes, that is, the Preacher [Latin *concionator*: one who addresses an assembly, *concio*]: for just as it belongs to a preacher to speak in the persons of many, and at last, by concluding and defining the judgement, to determine what is to be held, and in this way to calm the discord of a crowd that is in uproar and at variance with itself, so Solomon in this book speaks in the persons of diverse men, who hold and think diverse things. And he often defines what is to be held for salvation: indeed, at the end of the volume he sets out what all men must, of necessity for salvation, believe and do, saying: [[Eccles 12:13|Let us all hear together the conclusion of the discourse|Finem loquendi pariter omnes audiamus]]: [[Eccles 12:13|Fear God, and keep his commandments|Deum time, et mandata ejus observa]].

paras.t: Præmittit autem Salomon huic libro suo titulum istum : Verba Ecclesiastæ filii David regis Jerusalem : id est, verba sequentia, sunt verba ipsius Ecclesiastæ, utpote Salomonis filii David. Et quod ait, Regis, potest ad David et ad Salomonem referri. Et quoniam liber Proverbiorum specialiter circa parvulorum seu imperfectorum et incipientium instructionem versatur; ideo in illius libri titulo vocatur Salomon rex Israel, id est duodecim tribuum : per quas communis populus credentium, pro maxima sui parte imperfectus ac rudis, signatur. In prologo autem codicis hujus, rex Jerusalem appellatur : quia per Jerusalem, tanquam per metropolitas, id est principalis ac regiæ urbis habitatores, significantur proficientes, qui jam a vitiis expurgati atque moralibus virtutibus instituti, instruuntur et accenduntur in libro isto ad omnium terrenorum contemptum, invariabilisque boni considerationem ac veræ salutis affectum. Porro in prologo Cantici canticorum, ipse Salomon nec rex Israel, neque rex Jerusalem nuncupatur : quia in illo volumine perfectorum et theoricorum continetur instructio seu doctrina virorum, quorum se regem noluit designare, sed potius fratrem, ut ait Hieronymus, qui librum istum exposuit. Cujus expositionem Albinus in suo super librum istum commento, pro majori parte induxit, elucidavit ac dilatavit.
paras.en: Now Solomon sets this title before this book of his: [[1:1|The words of Ecclesiastes, the son of David, king of Jerusalem|Verba Ecclesiastæ filii David regis Jerusalem]]; that is, the words that follow are the words of Ecclesiastes himself, namely of Solomon, the son of David. And what he says, *king*, can be referred both to David and to Solomon. And since the book of Proverbs is concerned especially with the instruction of little ones, that is, of the imperfect and of beginners, in the title of that book Solomon is called king of Israel, that is, of the twelve tribes, by which is signified the common people of believers, for the greatest part imperfect and unlearned. But in the prologue of this volume he is called king of Jerusalem: for by Jerusalem, as by its metropolitans [that is, the citizens of the mother city], that is, the inhabitants of the chief and royal city, are signified those who are making progress, who, already cleansed of vices and formed in the moral virtues, are instructed and kindled in this book to contempt of all earthly things, to the consideration of the unchanging good, and to the desire of true salvation. Further, in the prologue of the Canticle of canticles Solomon himself is called neither king of Israel nor king of Jerusalem: for that volume contains the instruction or teaching of the perfect and contemplative [Latin *theorici*, from the Greek *theoria*, contemplation], of whom he did not wish to name himself king, but rather brother, as Jerome says, who expounded this book. His exposition Albinus [that is, Alcuin], in his own commentary on this book, for the greater part brought in, explained and enlarged.

paras.t: Ait quippe Hieronymus in expositione sua, quam ad S. Paulam Eustochiumque direxit : Quum Romæ essem, et sanctæ Blesillæ legerem Ecclesiasten, ut eam ad hujus mundi provocarem contemptum, et illa omne quod in mundo cernebat, pro nihilo reputaret, ab ea rogatus sum, ut obscura quæque libri hujus dissererem, quatenus absque mea præsentia posset intelligere quæ legebat. Itaque, quoniam ipsa in procinctu expositionis nostræ subita morte subtracta est, et non miremur, o Paula et Eustochium, talem vitæ nostræ habere consortem, tanto vulnere tristitiæ tunc percussus obmutui : nunc in Bethleem constitutus, memoriæ sanctæ illius et vobis, quod debeo, reddo.
paras.en: For Jerome says in his exposition, which he addressed to St. Paula and Eustochium: When I was at Rome and was reading Ecclesiastes with the holy Blesilla, to stir her to contempt of this world, so that she might count as nothing all that she saw in the world, I was asked by her to discuss whatever was obscure in this book, so that she might understand without my presence what she was reading. And so, since she was taken away by a sudden death while our exposition was in preparation, and we did not deserve, O Paula and Eustochium, to have such a companion of our life [the print reads *non miremur*, "let us not wonder"; Jerome's preface has *non meruimus*, "we did not deserve", which is followed here], I was struck dumb at the time by so great a wound of sorrow; now, settled in Bethlehem, I render to her holy memory and to you what I owe.

paras.t: Præterea ad intelligendum limpidius universa in libro isto contenta, advertenda sunt verba sancti Gregorii, quarto Dialogorum dicentis (cujus etiam verba Glossa et Albinus commemorant) : Ecclesiastes, inquit, Græce, concionator proprie dicitur. In concione vero sententia promitur, per quam tumultuosæ turbæ seditio comprimatur : et cum multi diversa sentiunt, per concionantis rationem ad unam sententiam perducuntur. Hic igitur liber idcirco concionator dicitur, quoniam Salomon in eo quasi tumultuantis turbæ assumpsit sensum, ut ea per inquisitionem diceret, quæ fortasse per tentationem imperita gens sentit. Quot enim sententias per inquisitionem movet, quasi tot in se personas diversorum accepit. Sed concionator verax quasi extenta manu tumultus omnium sedat, eosque ad unam sententiam revocat, quum in ejusdem libri termino ait : Finem loquendi omnes pariter audiamus : Deum time, etc. Si enim in libro isto per locutionem suam personas plurimorum non accepit, cur ad audiendum loquendi finem, omnes secum admonuit?
paras.en: Moreover, to understand more clearly all that this book contains, we must attend to the words of St. Gregory, who says in the fourth book of the Dialogues (whose words the Gloss and Albinus also recall): *Ecclesiastes*, he says, in Greek is properly called the Preacher. Now in an assembly a judgement is put forth by which the uproar of a tumultuous crowd may be put down; and when many think diverse things, they are brought to one judgement by the reasoning of the one who addresses them. This book, then, is called the Preacher because in it Solomon took on, as it were, the mind of a crowd in uproar, so as to say by way of inquiry the things which ignorant folk perhaps feel through temptation. For as many opinions as he raises by inquiry, so many persons of diverse men has he, as it were, taken upon himself. But the truthful preacher, as though with outstretched hand, calms the uproar of all and calls them back to one judgement, when at the end of the same book he says: [[Eccles 12:13|Let us all hear together the conclusion of the discourse|Finem loquendi omnes pariter audiamus]]: [[Eccles 12:13|Fear God|Deum time]], etc. For if in this book he had not taken on the persons of many in his speaking, why did he urge all, together with himself, to hear the conclusion of the discourse?

paras.t: Unde alia sunt quæ in libro isto per inquisitionem dicuntur, et alia quæ per rationem ad satisfaciendum promuntur; alia quæ ex persona hominis carnalis et tentati pronuntiantur, alia quæ ex rationis judicio proferuntur, ut animus a delectationibus compescatur. Nam infra ait : Hoc itaque mihi visum est bonum, ut comedat quis et bibat, et fruatur lætitia ex suo labore. Et tamen postea subdit : Melius est ire ad domum luctus, quam ad domum convivii. Si enim bonum est manducare et bibere, delectationeque frui, melius est ire ad domum convivii, quam ad domum luctus. Unde elicitur, quod illud ex infirmantium atque carnalium persona intulit, istud vero ex rationis definitione subjunxit. Nam et causam cur istud sit melius, addidit, dicens : In illa enim, scilicet in domo luctus, finis cunctorum admonetur hominum, et vivens cogitat quid futurum sit. Iterum ait : Lætare, juvenis, in adolescentia tua. Et tamen paulo post subdit : Adolescentia et voluptas vana sunt. Consimiliter concionator iste diversas tentationum cogitationes exprimens, ait : Unus est interitus hominum et jumentorum, et nihil habet homo jumento amplius. Sed ex rationis definitione postea dicit : Quid amplius habet sapiens a stulto? et quid pauper, nisi ut pergat illuc ubi est vita? In quibus verbis declarat quod hic non sit vera hominum vita, ad quam obtinendam pergit sapiens post hanc vitam. Postremo, concionator iste longe inferius loquitur : Quodcumque potest manus tua, instanter operare : quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia erunt apud inferos, quo tu properas. Quomodo ergo unus interitus est hominis et jumenti? aut quomodo nihil habet homo jumento amplius, quum jumenta post mortem carnis non vivant, spiritus autem hominum iniquorum post mortem carnis ad inferos deducantur? Has ergo tam diversas mentis humanæ opiniones, diligenter libri hujus lector consideret, et quid cui personæ conveniat, penset, ne in Epicuri errorem labatur, qui in delectationibus carnis summum bonum hominis fatebatur.
paras.en: Hence some things are said in this book by way of inquiry, and others are put forth by reason to give satisfaction; some are uttered in the person of a carnal and tempted man, others are brought forth from the judgement of reason, so that the mind may be restrained from pleasures. For further on he says: [[Eccles 5:17|This therefore hath seemed good to me, that a man should eat and drink|Hoc itaque mihi visum est bonum, ut comedat quis et bibat]], and enjoy gladness of his labour [Denis reads *fruatur lætitia ex suo labore*; the Douay-Rheims has "enjoy the fruit of his labour"]. And yet afterwards he adds: [[Eccles 7:3|It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to the house of feasting|Melius est ire ad domum luctus, quam ad domum convivii]]. For if it is good to eat and drink and to enjoy pleasure, it is better to go to the house of feasting than to the house of mourning. From this it follows that he brought in the former in the person of the weak and carnal, but added the latter from the definition of reason. For he also added the reason why the latter is better, saying: [[Eccles 7:3|for in that|In illa enim]], namely in the house of mourning, [[Eccles 7:3|we are put in mind of the end of all, and the living thinketh what is to come|finis cunctorum admonetur hominum, et vivens cogitat quid futurum sit]]. Again he says: [[Eccles 11:9|Rejoice|Lætare]], [[Eccles 11:9|O young man, in thy youth|juvenis, in adolescentia tua]]. And yet a little after he adds: [[Eccles 11:10|youth and pleasure are vain|Adolescentia et voluptas vana sunt]]. In the same way this preacher, expressing the diverse thoughts of temptations, says: [[Eccles 3:19|the death of man, and of beasts is one|Unus est interitus hominum et jumentorum]], [[Eccles 3:19|and man hath nothing more than beast|et nihil habet homo jumento amplius]]. But afterwards he says from the definition of reason: [[Eccles 6:8|What hath the wise man more than the fool? and what the poor man, but to go thither, where there is life?|Quid amplius habet sapiens a stulto? et quid pauper, nisi ut pergat illuc ubi est vita?]] In these words he declares that the true life of men is not here, to obtain which the wise man goes on after this life. Lastly, this preacher says much further on: [[Eccles 9:10|Whatsoever thy hand is able to do, do it earnestly: for neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge shall be in hell, whither thou art hastening|Quodcumque potest manus tua, instanter operare : quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia erunt apud inferos, quo tu properas]]. How then is the death of man and of beast one? Or how has man nothing more than beast, since beasts do not live after the death of the flesh, but the spirits of wicked men are led down to hell after the death of the flesh? Let the reader of this book, then, carefully consider these so diverse opinions of the human mind, and weigh which befits which person, lest he fall into the error of Epicurus, who held that man's highest good lies in the pleasures of the flesh.

paras.t: Insuper (sicut aliqui narrant) tempore Salomonis, studium sapientiæ in Jerusalem viguit, et circa hominis felicitatem diversi diversimode opinabantur, quibusdam eam ponentibus in temporalibus divitiis, aliis autem in carnalibus deliciis, aliis vero in mundanis honoribus, nonnullis demum in scientiis speculativis, aut practicis acquisitis, quibusdam quoque in vita præsenti, ceteris in futura. Ideo Salomon in hoc libro quæstionem hanc voluit pertractare, ostendendo quod in nullo talium, sed in solo Deo, humana consistat felicitas. Verumtamen Glossa et Albinus testantur, quod secundum Hebræos, Salomon fecit hunc librum pœnitens de suis peccatis, eo quod in sapientia sua divitiisque confisus, Deum per immunditiam idololatriamque valde offenderat.
paras.en: Besides (as some relate), in Solomon's time the study of wisdom flourished in Jerusalem, and various men held various opinions about man's happiness: some placed it in temporal riches, others in carnal delights, others again in worldly honours, some, lastly, in the acquired sciences, speculative or practical, some also in the present life, the rest in the life to come. So Solomon wished in this book to treat this question thoroughly, showing that human happiness consists in none of these, but in God alone. And yet the Gloss and Albinus bear witness that according to the Hebrews Solomon made this book as a penitent for his sins, because, trusting in his wisdom and his riches, he had greatly offended God by uncleanness and idolatry.

paras.t: Salomon ergo experientia longa edoctus, atque ad pristinæ sapientiæ lumen reversus, ex plenitudine internæ ac evidentissimæ considerationis variabilium ac sensibilium rerum, in hanc vocem repente erupit, et conclusionem quam probare voluit, in primis deprompsit, dicendo : Vanitas vanitatum, dixit Ecclesiastes. Et in signum assertionis ac confirmationis et seriositatis, repetivit et addidit : Vanitas vanitatum, et omnia vanitas : id est, omnia ista carnalia et transitoria et mundana, tot vitiis et pœnis, tot instabilitatibus atque miseriis, tot fallaciis et periculis, tot ignorantiis et inquietudinibus, laboribus, itemque doloribus sunt repleta, ut aptius dici valeant vanitas ipsa, quam vana : sicut de homine multum caro dicitur, Tu es amor meus; et de homine multum turbulento et inquieto, Tu es inquietudo et tribulatio nostra. Juxta quem modum in Proverbiis scriptum est : Gaudium patris, filius sapiens; filius stultus, mœstitia matris. Imo non solum possunt dici vanitas ipsa, sed et vanitas vanitatum, ut magnitudo ac multitudo vanitatis eorum insinuentur : sicut econtra dicuntur Cantica canticorum, quia inter cantica Scripturarum, excellentiam sortiuntur; et rosa, flos florum vocatur, quia pulcherrima inter flores; caritas quoque, virtus virtutum asseritur, utpote summa inter virtutes.
paras.en: So Solomon, taught by long experience and returned to the light of his former wisdom, out of the fullness of an inward and most evident consideration of changeable and sensible things, suddenly broke out into this cry, and set forth first of all the conclusion which he meant to prove, saying: [[1:2|Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes|Vanitas vanitatum, dixit Ecclesiastes]]. And as a sign of assertion, confirmation and earnestness he repeated it and added: [[1:2|vanity of vanities, and all is vanity|Vanitas vanitatum, et omnia vanitas]]: that is, all these carnal, passing and worldly things are so full of so many vices and pains, so many instabilities and miseries, so many deceits and dangers, so many ignorances and disquiets, labours and sorrows too, that they may more fittingly be called vanity itself than vain: as of a man who is very dear it is said, Thou art my love; and of a very turbulent and restless man, Thou art our disquiet and trouble. In the same manner it is written in Proverbs: The joy of the father, a wise son[[Prov 15:20||]]; a foolish son, the sorrow of the mother[[Prov 10:1||]] [the margin gives Prov. x, 1; xv, 20; Denis gives the sense loosely, with nouns in place of the verbs ("maketh glad"), to show a person called by the name of what he causes]. Indeed, they can be called not only vanity itself but even vanity of vanities, so that the greatness and the multitude of their vanity may be conveyed: just as, on the contrary, the Canticle of canticles is so called because it has the pre-eminence among the songs of the Scriptures; and the rose is called the flower of flowers, because it is the most beautiful among flowers; charity too is said to be the virtue of virtues, as the highest among the virtues.

paras.t: Denique universa creata, etiam intellectualia et incorruptibilia ac impassibilia, secundum se considerata, possunt vana vocari : Primo, quia in ipsis non consistit vera felicitas. — Secundo, quia ex nihilo facta sunt, et (quantum ex ipsis est) ad nihilum tenderent, nec ad momentum possent subsistere, nisi omnipotentia ac benevolentia Creatoris conservaret ea in esse, prout Augustinus libro de Civitate Dei fatetur, Damascenus quoque libro secundo. Unde Plato in primo Timæi inducit Creatorem superioribus creaturis loquentem : O dii deorum! quorum idem pater opifexque ego sum. Natura quidem (id est ex vestra natura) corruptibiles estis, sed mea voluntate incorruptibiles permanetis. — Tertio, quia respectu Creatoris, nullius momenti sunt, et potius non esse, quam esse censentur, ita quod solus Deus dicitur esse, et qui est. Qui in Exodo Moysi ait : Ego sum qui sum. Hæc dices filiis Israel : Qui est, misit me ad vos. Cui sanctus Job loquitur : Nonne tu qui solus es? Atque Psalmista, Substantia mea tanquam nihilum ante te. Deus enim gloriosus et adorandus, incomparabiliter et prorsus in infinitum omnem creaturam in omni perfectione, dignitate, et felicitate excedit : sicque omni creaturæ, etiam Beatis in patria, vanitas quædam inesse et competere perhibetur : quæ vanitas non est nisi distantia ac defectus a vero, increato, et incommutabili esse, prout Alexander de Hales et Dominus Antisiodorensis in Summis suis declarant. — Quarto, quoniam omni creaturæ quædam mutabilitas, imo et quædam mortalitas, fertur inesse : quoniam ad minus quædam actionum seu intellectionum et cogitationum vicissitudo, alternatio sive successio, saltem circa objecta creata, inest eis. Propter quod Apostolus loquens de Deo : Solus (inquit) habet immortalitatem, et lucem habitat inaccessibilem. Verumtamen comparatione creaturarum cœlestium perpetuarum et beatarum ac incorporalium, inferiora ista recte censentur plurimum vana.
paras.en: Further, all created things, even the intellectual, incorruptible and impassible, considered in themselves, can be called vain. First, because true happiness does not consist in them. Secondly, because they were made from nothing, and (as far as lies in them) would tend to nothing, and could not subsist for a moment unless the almighty power and goodness of the Creator kept them in being, as Augustine declares in the book of the City of God, and Damascene too in his second book. Hence Plato, in the first book of the Timaeus, brings in the Creator speaking to the higher creatures: O gods of gods, whose father and maker I am! By nature indeed (that is, of your own nature) you are corruptible, but by my will you remain incorruptible. Thirdly, because in respect of the Creator they are of no account, and are reckoned rather not to be than to be, so that God alone is said to be, and to be He who is. He it is who says to Moses in Exodus: [[Ex 3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]]. [[Ex 3:14|Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you|Hæc dices filiis Israel : Qui est, misit me ad vos]]. To Him holy Job says: [[Job 14:4|is it not thou who only art?|Nonne tu qui solus es?]] And the Psalmist: [[Ps 38:6|my substance is as nothing before thee|Substantia mea tanquam nihilum ante te]]. For God, glorious and to be adored, exceeds every creature incomparably and altogether infinitely in every perfection, dignity and happiness; and so a certain vanity is said to be in every creature and to belong to it, even to the Blessed in the fatherland: which vanity is nothing but distance from, and falling short of, true, uncreated and unchangeable being, as Alexander of Hales and the Lord of Auxerre [that is, William of Auxerre] declare in their Summas. Fourthly, because a certain changeableness, indeed a certain mortality, is said to be in every creature: since at the least there is in them a certain interchange, alternation or succession of actions, or of acts of understanding and of thoughts, at least about created objects. For which reason the Apostle, speaking of God, says: [[1 Tim 6:16|Who only|Solus]] (he says) [[1 Tim 6:16|hath immortality and inhabiteth light inaccessible|habet immortalitatem, et lucem habitat inaccessibilem]]. Nevertheless, in comparison with the heavenly creatures, everlasting, blessed and incorporeal, these lower things are rightly reckoned exceedingly vain.

paras.t: Sed his objici potest, quod in Genesi legitur, Vidit Deus cuncta quæ fecit, et erant valde bona : quomodo ergo vana et vanitas, imo vanitas vanitatum? Respondetur, quod in quantum aliquid de perfectione Creatoris participant, ac sibi invicem pulchre et sapienter ac multum utiliter coordinata exsistunt, valde bona dicuntur; nihilo minus, in quantum a Creatoris excellentia infinite deficiunt, et propter alias causas nunc introductas, vana et vanitas, vanitatumque vanitas nuncupantur. Unde ad Romanos fatur Apostolus : Vanitati creatura subjecta est. Atque de homine, principali creatura mundi inferioris, fertur in libro Psalmorum : Homo vanitati similis factus est; et rursus, Verumtamen universa vanitas omnis homo vivens. Ideo Isaias disseruit : Omnes gentes quasi non sint, sic sunt coram eo, et quasi nihilum et inane reputatæ sunt ei. Hoc, flagellis eruditus Nabuchodonosor (Daniele propheta testante) fatetur, dicendo : Omnes habitatores terræ apud ipsum in nihilum reputantur. Hinc, pro Vanitas vanitatum, aliqui transtulerunt, Vapor fumi et aura tenuis, quæ celeriter dissolvuntur, ut universa hæc, instar fumi transitoria designentur : sicut et Jacobus ait apostolus : Quæ est vita vestra? Vapor est ad modicum parens, deinceps exterminabitur.
paras.en: But against this it can be objected that we read in Genesis: [[Gen 1:31|God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good|Vidit Deus cuncta quæ fecit, et erant valde bona]]: how then are they vain and vanity, indeed vanity of vanities? The answer is that in so far as they share something of the Creator's perfection, and stand ordered to one another beautifully, wisely and very usefully, they are called very good; nevertheless, in so far as they fall infinitely short of the Creator's excellence, and for the other reasons just given, they are called vain and vanity, and vanity of vanities. Hence the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 8:20|the creature was made subject to vanity|Vanitati creatura subjecta est]]. And of man, the chief creature of the lower world, it is said in the book of Psalms: [[Ps 143:4|Man is like to vanity|Homo vanitati similis factus est]]; and again: [[Ps 38:6|And indeed all things are vanity: every man living|Verumtamen universa vanitas omnis homo vivens]]. So Isaias declared: [[Is 40:17|All nations are before him as if they had no being at all, and are counted to him as nothing, and vanity.|Omnes gentes quasi non sint, sic sunt coram eo, et quasi nihilum et inane reputatæ sunt ei]] This Nabuchodonosor, taught by scourges, confesses (as Daniel the prophet bears witness), saying: [[Dan 4:32|all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing before him|Omnes habitatores terræ apud ipsum in nihilum reputantur]]. Hence for [[1:2|Vanity of vanities|Vanitas vanitatum]] some have translated: Vapour of smoke and a thin breeze, which quickly dissolve [so Jerome in his commentary, rendering the Greek of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion], so that all these things may be shown to be passing like smoke: as the apostle James also says: [[Jas 4:15|what is your life? It is a vapour which appeareth for a little while and afterwards shall vanish away|Quæ est vita vestra? Vapor est ad modicum parens, deinceps exterminabitur]]

paras.t: Denique ex horum consideratione debemus nos semper humiliare, quia in nobis et ex nobis vani ac vanitas sumus, atque a Deo, quidquid boni habemus, accepimus, et ab ejus excellentia infinite deficimus, omnisque cultus, honor et reverentia, quos sibi gloriosissimo Creatori impendere possumus, in infinitum minores sunt cultu, honore et reverentia, quibus ipse dignissimus est.
paras.en: Lastly, from the consideration of these things we ought always to humble ourselves, because in ourselves and of ourselves we are vain and vanity, and whatever good we have we have received from God, and we fall infinitely short of His excellence; and all the worship, honour and reverence which we can pay to the most glorious Creator are infinitely less than the worship, honour and reverence of which He is most worthy.

paras.t: Quid habet amplius quam vanitatem, homo de universo labore suo, quo laborat sub sole, id est de laboribus quibus circa sensibilia atque carnalia occupatur ad acquirendum divitias, delicias, aut honores? Finaliter aliud nihil quam vanitatem consequitur. Unde in fine sero pœnitentes, dicturi sunt illud Sapientiæ : Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, et ambulavimus vias difficiles; viam autem Domini ignoravimus. Imo se taliter occupando, vani redduntur et hauriunt vanitatem. Hinc per Jeremiam loquitur Dominus : Quid invenerunt patres vestri in me iniquitatis, quia elongaverunt a me, et ambulaverunt post vanitatem, et vani facti sunt? Talibus clamat Psalmista : Filii hominum, usquequo gravi corde? ut quid diligitis vanitatem, et quæritis mendacium? Hinc uni talium in Evangelio dicitur : Stulte, hac nocte animam tuam repetunt a te : quæ autem parasti, cujus erunt? Quibus verbis adjecit Salvator : Sic est omnis qui non est in Deo dives.
paras.en: [[1:3|What hath a man more|Quid habet amplius]] than vanity [[1:3|of all his labour, that he taketh under the sun|homo de universo labore suo, quo laborat sub sole]], that is, of the labours with which he is busied about sensible and carnal things, to gain riches, delights or honours? In the end he gets nothing but vanity. Hence at the end, repenting too late, they will say that word of Wisdom: [[Wis 5:7|We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction, and have walked through hard ways, but the way of the Lord we have not known.|Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, et ambulavimus vias difficiles; viam autem Domini ignoravimus]] Indeed, by busying themselves in this way they are made vain, and drink in vanity. Hence the Lord says by Jeremias: [[Jer 2:5|What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me, and have walked after vanity, and are become vain?|Quid invenerunt patres vestri in me iniquitatis, quia elongaverunt a me, et ambulaverunt post vanitatem, et vani facti sunt?]] To such the Psalmist cries: [[Ps 4:3|O ye sons of men, how long will you be dull of heart? why do you love vanity, and seek after lying?|Filii hominum, usquequo gravi corde? ut quid diligitis vanitatem, et quæritis mendacium?]] Hence to one of these it is said in the Gospel: [[Luke 12:20|Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee. And whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?|Stulte, hac nocte animam tuam repetunt a te : quæ autem parasti, cujus erunt?]] To which words the Saviour added: [[Luke 12:21|So is|Sic est]] every one who [[Luke 12:21|is not rich towards God|non est in Deo dives]] [Denis reads *Sic est omnis qui non est in Deo dives*, without "that layeth up treasure for himself"].

paras.t: Generatio præterit, et generatio advenit : id est, quidam homines quotidie moriuntur, et alii de novo nascuntur, juxta verbum Job, quo ait : Conteret multos et innumerabiles, et stare faciet alios pro eis. Et Baruch : Exterminati sunt, inquit, et ad inferos descenderunt, et alii loco eorum surrexerunt. Terra autem elementum in æternum stat : id est, elementum terræ in medio universi perpetuo permanet fixum, ita quod, quoad se totum, nequit corrumpi. Et in hoc innotescit vanitas hominum, instabilitas sæculi, miseria mundi, quod homines propter quos facta est terra, moriuntur tam cito, et terra a parte post nunquam destruitur. Unde fertur in Psalmo : Etenim firmavit orbem terræ, qui non commovebitur. — Mystice, præteriit generatio idololatrarum, advenit generatio Judæorum, deinde natio tyrannorum et persecutorum, supervenit quoque generatio varia hæreticorum : nihilo minus terra, id est Ecclesia militans, usque ad finem mundi persistit in fide et caritate.
paras.en: [[1:4|One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh|Generatio præterit, et generatio advenit]]: that is, some men die every day, and others are newly born, according to the word of Job, where he says: [[Job 34:24|He shall break in pieces many and innumerable, and shall make others to stand in their stead|Conteret multos et innumerabiles, et stare faciet alios pro eis]] [the margin gives Job xxxiv, 21; the words are Job 34:24]. And Baruch: [[Bar 3:19|They are cut off|Exterminati sunt]], he says, [[Bar 3:19|and are gone down to hell, and others are risen up in their place|et ad inferos descenderunt, et alii loco eorum surrexerunt]]. [[1:4|but the earth|Terra autem]], the element, [[1:4|standeth for ever|in æternum stat]]: that is, the element of earth abides for ever fixed in the middle of the universe, so that, taken as a whole, it cannot be corrupted. And in this the vanity of men, the instability of the age and the misery of the world are made known: that men, for whose sake the earth was made, die so soon, while the earth is never destroyed hereafter [Latin *a parte post*, a scholastic phrase: on the side of what comes after]. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 92:1|For he hath established the world which shall not be moved|Etenim firmavit orbem terræ, qui non commovebitur]]. Mystically, the generation of idolaters passed away, the generation of the Jews came; then the nation of tyrants and persecutors; there followed also the motley generation of heretics: nevertheless the earth, that is, the Church militant, endures in faith and charity until the end of the world.

paras.t: Oritur sol omni die de mane super horizontem nostrum, motu diurno, quem habet ex circumvolutione primi mobilis, suo impetu secum rapientis et circummoventis sphæras inferiores cum suis sideribus et planetis; et occidit, descendendo ab axe poli, et ad locum suum, videlicet orientem, revertitur; ibique renascens, id est iterum nobis oriens et apparens, gyrat per meridiem, id est, circumeundo declinat versus partes australes et ad polum antarcticum, præsertim in hieme, et tanto plus, quanto dies sunt breviores; et flectitur ad aquilonem, redeundo ad orientem. Itaque sol, qui ad producendum diem hominibus datus est, et ad alia commoda, suo ortu et occasu quotidie lapsum et alterationem mundi inferioris monstrat et causat : qui per abditas vias ab occidente in orientem regreditur, expletoque circulo suo, quasi de thalamo novus exsurgit. Quod Salomon ideo tangit, ut doceat nos, variationibus temporum, et ortu occasuque solis ac siderum, vitam labi humanam, et senescere hominem, dum non pensat. Nempe (ut Aristoteles probat) sol motu suo in circulo obliquo, id est zodiaco, causa est alterationis, generationis et corruptionis in elementis et mixtis. Obliqua etenim linea est zona zodiaci circuli, per quam cursus est solis. Idcirco brumali (id est hiemali) tempore ad australia, id est ad meridiem, divexo tramite vergit sol, et denuo in æstate ad borealia, id est aquilonem, se flectit, ne sole uno modo currente, alia calor consumeret, alia frigus destrueret. Hinc subditur :
paras.en: [[1:5|The sun riseth|Oritur sol]] every day in the morning above our horizon, by the daily motion which it has from the revolution of the first movable [that is, the outermost sphere, which by its daily turning carries the lower spheres with it], which by its force sweeps along with it and carries round the lower spheres with their stars and planets; [[1:5|and goeth down|et occidit]], descending from the axis of the pole; [[1:5|and returneth|revertitur]] [[1:5|to his place|et ad locum suum]], namely the east; [[1:5|and there rising again|ibique renascens]], that is, rising and appearing to us again, [[1:6|Maketh his round by the south|gyrat per meridiem]], that is, going round, it bends towards the southern parts and the antarctic pole, especially in winter, and the more so the shorter the days are; [[1:6|and turneth again to the north|et flectitur ad aquilonem]], returning towards the east. And so the sun, which was given to men to bring forth the day, and for other benefits, by its rising and setting every day shows and causes the passing and alteration of the lower world: it goes back by hidden ways from the west to the east, and, its circle completed, rises anew as from a bridechamber. Solomon touches on this to teach us that by the changes of the seasons, and the rising and setting of the sun and stars, human life slips away and man grows old while he does not consider it. For (as Aristotle proves) the sun, by its motion in the oblique circle, that is, the zodiac, is the cause of alteration, generation and corruption in the elements and in mixed bodies. For the belt of the zodiac, along which the sun runs its course, is an oblique line. Therefore in the winter season the sun inclines by a sloping path towards the southern parts, that is, towards the south, and in summer bends again towards the northern parts, that is, the north, lest, if the sun ran always in one way, heat should consume some things and cold destroy others. Hence there follows:

paras.t: Lustrans, id est illuminans, universa corporalia, lucis suæ capacia, in circuitu mundi inferioris, et sphærarum sub se contentarum, pergit, id est, movetur et circuit, spiritus, id est sol, et in circulos suos revertitur. Singulis namque diebus completur ac mutatur circulatio solis, id est circularis circuitio ejus, qua jugiter magis propinquat vel ad tropicum æstivalem, aut certe ad tropicum hiemalem. Sicque dum sol maxime declinaverit, rursus per eosdem circulos seu meatus in zodiaco ascendit. Et quum summe ascenderit, mox rursus incipit declinare. Aut ideo dicitur sol in circulos suos reverti, quia (secundum Ptolemæum et alios) sol circulos habet plures, in quibus movetur, puta æquantem, epicyclum, atque eccentricum, sicut de hoc Albategni, Albumasar et alii scribunt diffusius.
paras.en: [[1:6|surveying|Lustrans]], that is, illuminating, [[1:6|all places|universa]], all bodily things that can receive its light, [[1:6|round about|in circuitu]] the lower world and the spheres contained beneath it, [[1:6|goeth forward|pergit]], that is, moves and goes round, [[1:6|the spirit|spiritus]], that is, the sun, [[1:6|and returneth to his circuits|et in circulos suos revertitur]]. For each day the circling of the sun, that is, its circular course, is completed and changed, by which it comes continually nearer either to the summer tropic or to the winter tropic. And so, when the sun has declined to the utmost, it climbs again by the same circles or paths in the zodiac; and when it has climbed to the highest, it soon begins again to decline. Or the sun is said to return to its circles because (according to Ptolemy and others) the sun has several circles in which it moves, namely the equant, the epicycle and the eccentric, as Albategni, Albumasar and others write of this at greater length.

paras.t: Porro (secundum Albinum et Glossam) Salomon solem nominat spiritum, quoniam animat, inspirat et vivificat inferiora, id est, per lumen, motum et influentiam suam, causat in animalibus et mixtis animationem, spirationem et vitam. Quod etiam magnus Dionysius, quarto capitulo de Divinis nominibus, protestatur. Propter quod ait Philosophus, quod homo generat hominem, et sol : homo tanquam agens particulare, sol tanquam agens universale. Verumtamen S. Hieronymus circa hunc locum ait : Ipsum solem spiritum nominat, quod animalis sit, et spiret et vigeat. Quocirca multa et magna posset inquisitio fieri. De hoc tamen, an corpora cœlestia sint animata, B. Hieronymus super Isaiam, ambigue loquitur, et magis ad hoc declinare videtur, quod non. Augustinus vero super Genesim ad litteram, et in Enchiridion dicit de hac re esse grandem et abditam quæstionem, quæ nec refutanda sit, quousque falsitas ejus certius innotescat, nec acceptanda, donec ejus veritas clarius elucescat; seque ambigere, an ad Beatorum et angelorum societatem pertineant sol et luna, ac cetera astra. Rabbi Moyses vero asserit corpora cœlestia esse animata, et Creatorem suum sublimibus canticis esse laudantia : quod affirmat ex lege et Prophetis probari. Sanctus vero Basilius et Damascenus dicunt omnino contrarium. Thomas autem, quamvis super secundum Sententiarum in hoc Basilium et Damascenum sequatur, tamen in Summa contra gentiles, in qua magistralius atque subtilius loquitur, dicit ad christianam Religionem non differre nec pertinere, quidquid horum dicatur. Nihilo minus puto securius, ad hoc magis divertere, ut dicantur animata non esse. Sed de hoc hic tantumdem tetigisse sufficiat, de quo Thomas in Summa contra gentiles, et Albertus libro de IV Coæquævis, diligenter subtiliterque loquuntur. Porro Symmachus pro Spiritu transtulit Ventum.
paras.en: Further (according to Albinus and the Gloss), Solomon calls the sun *spirit* because it animates, inspires and quickens the lower things: that is, by its light, motion and influence it causes animation, breathing and life in living things and in mixed bodies. The great Dionysius also affirms this, in the fourth chapter of the Divine Names. For this reason the Philosopher says that man begets man, and the sun too: man as a particular agent, the sun as a universal agent. Nevertheless St. Jerome says on this place: He calls the sun itself *spirit* because it is a living thing, and breathes and has vigour. On this a long and great inquiry could be made. As to whether the heavenly bodies are animate, however, Blessed Jerome on Isaias speaks doubtfully, and seems rather to lean to the view that they are not. Augustine, in the Literal Commentary on Genesis and in the Enchiridion, says that this is a great and hidden question, which is neither to be rejected until its falsity is known more surely, nor accepted until its truth shines out more clearly; and that he is in doubt whether the sun and moon and the other stars belong to the company of the Blessed and the angels. Rabbi Moyses [that is, Maimonides] asserts that the heavenly bodies are animate and praise their Creator with sublime songs, which he affirms is proved from the Law and the Prophets. St. Basil and Damascene say altogether the contrary. Thomas, though on the second book of the Sentences he follows Basil and Damascene in this, yet in the Summa contra Gentiles, where he speaks in a more masterly and subtle way, says that it makes no difference to the Christian religion, and does not concern it, which of these is said. Nevertheless I think it safer to incline rather to this, that they be said not to be animate. But let it suffice to have touched on this much here; Thomas in the Summa contra Gentiles and Albert in the book on the Four Coevals [that is, the four things created together at the beginning: matter, time, the empyrean heaven and the angelic nature] speak of it carefully and subtly. Further, Symmachus translated *Wind* for *Spirit*.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, sol justitiæ Christus oritur electis et bonis, occidit reprobis et injustis, et venit de summo cœlo in terram, atque in Ascensione ad suum rediit locum; ibique renascens, id est inde radios suæ illuminationis diffundens, undique visitat in meridie habitantes, id est in divini amoris fervore. Indeque transit ad aquilonem, id est ad frigidos et iniquos, quos admonet sæpe; et quos ex eis elegit, attrahit sibi.
paras.en: Spiritually, Christ, the sun of justice, rises for the elect and the good and sets for the reprobate and unjust; and He came from the highest heaven to earth, and in the Ascension returned to His place; and there rising again, that is, pouring forth from there the rays of His enlightening, He visits on every side those who dwell in the south, that is, in the fervour of divine love. And from there He passes to the north, that is, to the cold and wicked, whom He often admonishes; and those of them whom He has chosen He draws to Himself.

paras.t: Omnia flumina intrant in mare. Sicut enim principium, ortum, originem fontaliter habent ex magno mari per subterraneas venas, occultasve vias, seu evidentes meatus; sic tandem revertuntur in illud. Quod de notabiliter magnis fluminibus potissime verificatur : quæ etsi interdum videantur absorberi a terra, rursus tamen erumpunt alicubi, et in Oceanum refluunt; ac rursus ex Oceano aquæ derivantur ad terram per alia ac diversa itinera. Hinc subditur : Ad locum unde exeunt flumina, puta ad Oceanum, revertuntur ut iterum fluant. Hinc asserit Thomas super secundum Sententiarum, quod et fons paradisi, qui in quatuor capita et magna flumina dividitur, ex Oceano ducit originem. Verumtamen mare non redundat, id est, ex tali refluxu aquarum in ipsum, terminos suos non exit. Circa hoc dicit glossa Albini : Dicunt philosophi, dulces aquas quæ mari influunt, ardente sole consumi, vel salsuginis maris pabula esse; sed Ecclesiastes noster dicit, eas per occultas terræ venas ad capita fontium regredi, et de matrice abysso in sua semper ebullire principia. Verumtamen istud a dictis philosophorum non dissonat : quia et multi præclari philosophi asserunt, quod de mari per subterranea loca effluant aquæ ad loca remota : quæ aquæ in tantum naturaliter possunt ascendere, quantum alta est superficies maris, imo et altius, quoniam per terram manando, ipsa sua colatione dulciores redduntur et leviores aquis maris. Propterea in certis locis erumpunt in fontes et flumina : ex quibus locis tanquam altioribus quadam parte superficiei abyssi, rursus naturali motu in pelagus refluunt. Et hoc totum ad communem humani generis utilitatem, ita disposuit infinita, omnipotens, et benevolentissima sapientia Creatoris.
paras.en: [[1:7|All the rivers run into the sea|Omnia flumina intrant in mare]]. For just as they have their beginning, rise and origin, as from a fountainhead, out of the great sea, through underground veins, or hidden ways, or open channels, so at length they return into it. This is borne out above all in the notably great rivers: though at times they seem to be swallowed up by the earth, yet they break forth again somewhere and flow back into the Ocean; and again waters are drawn off from the Ocean to the land by other and different routes. Hence it is added: [[1:7|unto the place from whence the rivers come|Ad locum unde exeunt flumina]], namely to the Ocean, [[1:7|they return, to flow again|revertuntur ut iterum fluant]]. Hence Thomas asserts, on the second book of the Sentences, that the fountain of paradise too, which is divided into four heads and great rivers, takes its origin from the Ocean. Yet [[1:7|the sea doth not overflow|mare non redundat]], that is, it does not go beyond its bounds through such a flowing back of the waters into it. On this the gloss of Albinus [that is, Alcuin] says: The philosophers say that the sweet waters which flow into the sea are consumed by the burning sun, or are food for the saltness of the sea; but our Ecclesiastes says that they go back through hidden veins of the earth to the heads of the springs, and from the mother abyss are ever bubbling up into their sources. Yet this is not at odds with the sayings of the philosophers: for many eminent philosophers also assert that waters flow out from the sea through underground places to distant places; and these waters can naturally rise as high as the surface of the sea is high, and even higher, since by seeping through the earth they are made sweeter and lighter than the waters of the sea by this very straining. Therefore in certain places they break out into springs and rivers, and from these places, as being higher than some part of the surface of the abyss, they flow back again by natural motion into the deep sea. And all this the infinite, almighty and most benevolent wisdom of the Creator has so arranged for the common benefit of the human race.

paras.t: Spiritualiter. Omnia flumina intrant in mare, id est, universa gratiarum fluenta descendunt in cor humanum, quod instar maris, profundum ac imperscrutabile exstat. Et mare non redundat, id est, cor humanum ex hoc præfixos sibi limites non transcendit, inaniter gloriando aut se jactando vel intumescendo : imo magis humiliat se, et fonti gratiarum tanto plus gratum ac subjectum esse conatur, quanto plura et majora ab ipso beneficia accepisse se intuetur. Ad locum unde exeunt flumina revertuntur : id est, sicut universa gratiæ dona a Deo fontaliter oriuntur, sic ei cum gratiarum actione sunt adscribenda, et de omnibus ac in omnibus laudandus et glorificandus est universorum largitor bonorum. Ideo dicit Apostolus : Quid habes quod non accepisti? et item, Gratia Dei sum id quod sum : itemque, Soli Deo honor et gloria. Ut iterum fluant, id est, copiosius a Deo procedant. Dum enim de acceptis muneribus Deo grati consistimus, majora ab ipso suscipimus : quia, ut ait Salvator, Habenti dabitur, et abundabit. Optima ergo custos gratiarum est beneficiorum memoria, et recognitio eorumdem assidua, quæ abundantiora meretur charismata. Ingratitudo vero, tanquam ventus urens ac pestilens, fontem pietatis et gratiæ desiccat et obstruit ipsi ingrato.
paras.en: Spiritually. [[1:7|All the rivers run into the sea|Omnia flumina intrant in mare]], that is, all the streams of graces come down into the human heart, which, like the sea, is deep and unsearchable[[Jer 17:9||]]. [[1:7|yet the sea doth not overflow|Et mare non redundat]], that is, the human heart does not on this account pass beyond the limits set for it, by vainly glorying or boasting or swelling up; rather it humbles itself the more, and strives to be the more grateful and subject to the fountain of graces, the more and greater the benefits it sees it has received from him. [[1:7|unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return|Ad locum unde exeunt flumina revertuntur]]: that is, as all the gifts of grace spring from God as from their fountain, so they are to be ascribed to him with thanksgiving, and for all things and in all things the giver of all good things is to be praised and glorified. Therefore the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 4:7|what hast thou that thou hast not received|Quid habes quod non accepisti]]? and again: [[1 Cor 15:10|by the grace of God, I am what I am|Gratia Dei sum id quod sum]]; and again: To [[1 Tim 1:17|the only God, be honour and glory|Soli Deo honor et gloria]]. [[1:7|to flow again|Ut iterum fluant]], that is, that they may come forth from God more abundantly. For while we remain grateful to God for the gifts we have received, we receive greater ones from him; for, as the Saviour says, [[Matt 13:12|he that hath, to him shall be given, and he shall abound|Habenti dabitur, et abundabit]]. The best keeper of graces, then, is the remembrance of benefits and the constant acknowledgement of them, which merits more abundant gifts. Ingratitude, on the other hand, like a burning and pestilent wind, dries up and stops the fountain of mercy and grace for the ungrateful man himself.

paras.t: Cuncta res difficiles, ad intelligendum perfecte. Vix enim est aliqua creatura tam modica, de qua poterimus reddere rationem in singulis quæ possunt quæri de ea, et cujus propriam differentiam, universasque proprietates, causas et vires assignare poterimus. Ideo scriptum est : Difficile invenimus quæ in terra sunt; et quæ in prospectu sunt, invenimus cum difficultate. Non potest eas homo explicare sermone, expressione perfecte notificante rem ipsam, quia non valemus perfecte intelligere eas. Imo locutio deficit a plena repræsentatione notitiæ. Horum ratio assignatur, quoniam nostra cognitio intellectiva incipit a cognitione sensitiva et a posteriori, atque a notitia accidentium rei, in quibus natura agentis non relucet plenarie. Communiter tamen tenent philosophi, humanum intellectum posse in vita hac ad cognitionem quidditatis substantiarum materialium pervenire. Aliqui vero addunt, quod etiam ad cognitionem quidditatis substantiæ separatæ, posset in vita ista pertingere : cujus opinionis sunt Albertus, Ulricus, et alii quidam. Alii econtrario, ut Scotus, affirmant intellectum nostrum in hac vita perduci non posse ad alicujus rei creatæ cognitionem distinctam essentiæ. Cujus signum dicit Scotus esse, quod si simul ponantur duæ hostiæ, quarum una sit consecrata, alia non, non potest homo per naturalem rationem inter eas discernere.
paras.en: [[1:8|All things are hard|Cuncta res difficiles]], to understand perfectly. For there is scarcely any creature so small that we can give an account of it in every particular that can be asked about it, and assign its proper difference [that is, the specific difference that sets it apart from other things of its kind], and all its properties, causes and powers. Therefore it is written: [[Wis 9:16|hardly do we guess aright at things that are upon earth: and with labour do we find the things that are before us|Difficile invenimus quæ in terra sunt; et quæ in prospectu sunt, invenimus cum difficultate]] [Denis's wording, "we find", differs from the Vulgate's "we guess"]. [[1:8|man cannot explain them by word|Non potest eas homo explicare sermone]], by an expression that makes the thing itself perfectly known, because we cannot understand them perfectly. Indeed, speech falls short of fully representing our knowledge. The reason for these things is given: our intellectual knowledge begins from the knowledge of the senses, and a posteriori [that is, from effects rather than from causes], and from the knowledge of a thing's accidents, in which the nature of the agent does not shine out fully. Yet the philosophers commonly hold that the human intellect can in this life reach knowledge of the quiddity [that is, the essence, what a thing is] of material substances. Some add that it could in this life attain even to knowledge of the quiddity of a separate substance [that is, a pure spirit, such as an angel]: of this opinion are Albert, Ulric and certain others. Others on the contrary, like Scotus, affirm that in this life our intellect cannot be brought to a distinct knowledge of the essence of any created thing. A sign of this, Scotus says, is that if two hosts are set side by side, one of them consecrated and the other not, a man cannot tell them apart by natural reason.

paras.t: Non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris auditu impletur : id est, quantumcumque multa et magna videat oculus corporalis, potest et appetit plura videre. Similiter est de aure. Imo oculus nova et curiosa videndo, sæpe plus inflammatur ad plura hujusmodi intuenda : simili modo auditus. Conformiter interior oculus, scilicet intellectus, cognitionibus et scientiis rerum creatarum non saturatur nec quietatur; nec potest quiescere, nisi in notitia Creatoris. Non ergo in creatis, sed in Creatore, consistit felicitas.
paras.en: [[1:8|The eye is not filled with seeing, neither is the ear filled with hearing|Non saturatur oculus visu, nec auris auditu impletur]]: that is, however many and great the things the bodily eye sees, it can see more and desires to. So too with the ear. Indeed the eye, by seeing new and curious things, is often the more inflamed to look upon more such things; and likewise the hearing. In the same way the inner eye, that is, the intellect, is not filled nor set at rest by the knowledge and sciences of created things; nor can it rest except in the knowledge of the Creator. Happiness, then, consists not in creatures but in the Creator.

paras.t: Jam ergo demonstravit instabilitatem et variabilitatem assiduam in hominibus cœlestibusque corporibus et in aquis. Consequenter idem nunc ostendit in ceteris generabilibus et corruptibilibus. Quid est quod fuit, id est res generata quæ aliquando fuit, et modo non est? Ad quod respondet : Ipsum quod futurum est, id est, res illa præterita, est ipsa res futura : non utique eadem numero, sed specie, sicut homo mortuus, et homo nasciturus, ejusdem naturæ sunt, non una eademque persona. Et multo minus in irrationalibus animalibus, vegetabilibus, et mixtis, quorum formæ substantiales seu animæ sunt corruptibiles et mortales, desinentes esse in ipsa corporea morte. Hinc libro de Generatione et corruptione probat Philosophus, quod corrupta non redeunt eadem numero : naturaliter utique, sed miraculose fieri potest, et factum est sæpe, præsertim in evangelica lege. Quid est quod factum est? Respondet : Ipsum quod faciendum est, id est, ejusdem speciei utrumque est, sicut leo natus, et leo nasciturus.
paras.en: So far, then, he has shown the constant instability and changeableness in men, in the heavenly bodies and in the waters. Next he now shows the same in the other things subject to generation and corruption. [[1:9|What is it that hath been?|Quid est quod fuit]] that is, a thing generated which once was and now is not? To this he answers: [[1:9|the same thing that shall be|Ipsum quod futurum est]], that is, that past thing is the very thing to come: not indeed the same in number, but in species; as a man who has died and a man yet to be born are of the same nature, not one and the same person. And much less is it so in irrational animals, plants and mixed bodies [that is, bodies compounded of the elements], whose substantial forms or souls are corruptible and mortal, ceasing to be in bodily death itself. Hence in the book On Generation and Corruption the Philosopher proves that things corrupted do not return the same in number: naturally, that is; but it can happen by miracle, and has often happened, especially under the law of the Gospel. [[1:9|What is it that hath been done?|Quid est quod factum est?]] He answers: [[1:9|the same that shall be done|Ipsum quod faciendum est]], that is, both are of the same species, as a lion born and a lion yet to be born.

paras.t: Nihil sub sole novum, quum simile ejus in specie præcesserit. Nec valet quisquam dicere vere et rationabiliter : Ecce hoc recens est, id est individuum alicujus speciei, cujus simile non præcessit, loquendo de inferioribus istis. Ideo subditur : jam enim præcessit in sæculis quæ fuerunt ante nos : id est, in generationibus et periodis seu temporibus præteritis fuit simile ejus in specie. Juxta hunc modum dicimus non esse novum, dum videmus justos ab impiis infestari, homicidium fieri, hominem mori : quoniam ista, id est similia eis in specie, multoties contigerunt. Hinc quoque scriptum est : Complevit Deus die septimo opus suum quod fecerat, et requievit ab omni opere quod patrarat : non utique ex tunc usque in præsens, a productione novorum individuorum et suppositorum, sed speciei novarum, quia deinceps nihil produxit, cujus simile in specie in operibus sex dierum non præcessit.
paras.en: [[1:10|Nothing under the sun is new|Nihil sub sole novum]], since its like in species has gone before. [[1:10|neither is any man able to say|Nec valet quisquam dicere]] truly and reasonably: [[1:10|Behold this is new|Ecce hoc recens est]], that is, an individual of some species whose like has not gone before, speaking of these lower things. Therefore it is added: [[1:10|for it hath already gone before in the ages that were before us|jam enim præcessit in sæculis quæ fuerunt ante nos]]: that is, in past generations and periods or times there was its like in species. In this way we say it is nothing new when we see the just harassed by the wicked, murder done, a man die: because these things, that is, things like them in species, have happened many times. Hence too it is written: [[Gen 2:2|on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made|Complevit Deus die septimo opus suum quod fecerat]]: [[Gen 2:2|and he rested|et requievit]] [[Gen 2:2|from all his work which he had done|ab omni opere quod patrarat]]: not indeed from the production of new individuals and supposits [that is, individual subsisting beings] from then until now, but from that of new species; for afterwards he produced nothing whose like in species had not gone before in the works of the six days.

paras.t: Itaque locus iste Scripturæ, intelligendus est sane, ne quis sumat ex eo gravissimorum occasionem errorum, et putet cum Epicuro et Platone, eadem numero in mundo hoc renovari post certas periodos, aut post magni anni revolutionem. De qua Platonis opinione multa recitat Augustinus libro de Civitate Dei, et quædam in libro de Trinitate, sicut tangetur in fine expositionis hujus capituli. Nec iteratio ista consimilium in specie, intelligenda est de supernaturalibus et miraculosis effectibus, sed juxta expositionem præinductam, de mixtis generabilibus et corruptibilibus naturalibus. Ideo ait Hieronymus: Non putemus signa atque prodigia et multa quæ arbitrio Dei nova in mundo fiunt, in prioribus sæculis præcessisse, et locum invenire Epicurum, qui affirmat per innumerabiles periodos eadem his in locis et per eosdem fieri. Alioqui Judas crebro tradidit Christum, et Christus sæpe pro nobis est passus; et cetera quæ facta sunt et futura, in easdem similiter periodos revolvuntur. Sed dicendum, quod præscientia et prædestinatione Dei, ea jam facta sunt, quæ futura sunt. Præterea error ille, dicentium eadem numero taliter renovari atque redire, contrariatur Scripturæ, et in libro Job multipliciter reprobatur, ut quum ibidem sanctus Job loquitur: Viam per quam non revertar, ambulo: et rursus: Homo quum dormierit, non resurget: donec atteratur cœlum, non evigilabit. Nec pœna inferni esset perpetua, juxta illam insaniam.
paras.en: This passage of Scripture, then, must be understood soundly, lest anyone take from it occasion for the gravest errors and think, with Epicurus and Plato, that the same things in number are renewed in this world after certain periods, or after the revolution of the great year [that is, the vast cycle after which, on this view, the heavens return to the same position and all things begin over again]. Augustine recounts much of this opinion of Plato in the book of the City of God, and some things in the book on the Trinity, as will be touched on at the end of the exposition of this chapter. Nor is this repetition of things alike in species to be understood of supernatural and miraculous effects, but, according to the exposition given above, of natural mixed bodies subject to generation and corruption. Therefore Jerome says: Let us not think that signs and wonders, and the many things that are done new in the world at the will of God, went before in former ages, and that room is found for Epicurus, who affirms that through innumerable periods the same things are done in these places and by the same persons. Otherwise Judas has often betrayed Christ, and Christ has often suffered for us; and all the other things that have been done and are to come revolve likewise into the same periods. But it must be said that in the foreknowledge and predestination of God the things that are to come have already been done. Moreover, that error of those who say that the same things in number are renewed and return in this way is contrary to Scripture, and is refuted in many ways in the book of Job, as when holy Job says there: [[Job 16:23|I am walking in a path by which I shall not return|Viam per quam non revertar, ambulo]]; and again: [[Job 14:12|man when he is fallen asleep shall not rise again; till the heavens be broken, he shall not awake|Homo quum dormierit, non resurget: donec atteratur cœlum, non evigilabit]]. Nor, according to that madness, would the punishment of hell be everlasting.

paras.t: Non est priorum memoria: id est, illi qui nunc vivunt, non habent memoriam multarum rerum præteritarum. Sed nec eorum quidem, quæ postea futura sunt, erit recordatio apud eos qui futuri sunt in novissimo, id est in tempore valde longo post eos: quia et ipsi obliviscentur præteritorum, sicut et nos. Ex quibus ostenditur inconstantia rerum et memoriarum hominum in hoc mundo, et quod vanum sit constituere salutem in ista permanentia, qua homo post mortem manet in recordatione et laudibus hominum. Unde pro magna fama post mortem in hoc mundo habenda, multi plurimum laboraverunt.
paras.en: [[1:11|There is no remembrance of former things|Non est priorum memoria]]: that is, those who live now have no memory of many past things. [[1:11|nor indeed of those things which hereafter are to come, shall there be any remembrance with them that shall be in the latter end|Sed nec eorum quidem, quæ postea futura sunt, erit recordatio apud eos qui futuri sunt in novissimo]], that is, in a time very long after them: because they too will forget the things past, as we do. By this is shown the inconstancy of things and of men's memories in this world, and that it is vain to set one's well-being in that kind of lasting by which a man remains after death in the remembrance and praises of men. And yet, to have great fame in this world after death, many have laboured very hard.

paras.t: Consequenter Salomon sui ipsius exemplo declarat vera esse quæ dixit, scilicet omnia esse vana. Ego Ecclesiastes fui rex Israel in Jerusalem. Quare adhuc vivens non ait, Ego Ecclesiastes sum rex Israel in Jerusalem? Dicunt quidam, quod pœnitentiam agens, ex humilitate ita locutus est, quasi indignum se reputans nomine regis, qui populum suum tam enormiter male vivendo scandalizavit. Vel dicendo, Fui rex, non exclusit se esse regem: sed ideo ait, Fui rex, quia recitat gesta sua præterita. Aliqui quoque reges Juda ante mortem suam resignaverunt filiis suis regnum.
paras.en: Next Solomon declares by his own example that what he has said is true, namely that all things are vain. [[1:12|I Ecclesiastes was king over Israel in Jerusalem|Ego Ecclesiastes fui rex Israel in Jerusalem]]. Why, while still living, does he not say: I Ecclesiastes am king over Israel in Jerusalem? Some say that, doing penance, he spoke so out of humility, as though reckoning himself unworthy of the name of king, having so grievously scandalized his people by his evil life. Or else, in saying "I was king", he did not deny that he was king: he says "I was king" because he is relating his past deeds. Some kings of Juda, too, resigned the kingdom to their sons before their death.

paras.t: Et proposui in animo meo quærere, studendo, seu alios interrogando, et investigare sapienter de omnibus quæ fiunt sub sole, id est de causis et rationibus omnium talium, præsertim humanorum eventuum: scilicet cur quidam sic prosperantur, et diu vivunt; alii adversitatibus et diffortuniis opprimuntur: cur aliqui virtuosi utilesque prælati et principes cito tolluntur de medio: alii vitiosi præsidentes, subditisque nocivi, diu vivunt, et præsunt: cur quædam animæ infunduntur corpusculis infantulorum gentilium, nec unquam perducuntur ad fidei sacramentum; quædam vero animæ infunduntur corpusculis puerorum fidelium. Quamvis enim Salomon habuit de naturalibus, et multis supernaturalibus ac mysticis infusam scientiam, non tamen de omnibus talibus occultis Dei judiciis: de quibus immoderate scrutari, curiosum temerariumque censetur, quia omnino transcendit humanæ imbecillitatis capacitatem. Idcirco de talibus cum Apostolo est dicendum: O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, et investigabiles viæ ejus! et cum Psalmista, Judicia tua abyssus multa.
paras.en: [[1:13|And I proposed in my mind to seek|Et proposui in animo meo quærere]], by study or by asking others, [[1:13|and search out wisely concerning all things that are done under the sun|et investigare sapienter de omnibus quæ fiunt sub sole]], that is, concerning the causes and reasons of all such things, above all of human events: namely, why some prosper so and live long, while others are crushed by adversities and misfortunes; why some virtuous and useful prelates and princes are quickly taken from our midst, while other vicious rulers, harmful to their subjects, live long and stay in office; why some souls are infused into the little bodies of the infants of heathens and are never brought to the sacrament of faith, while other souls are infused into the little bodies of the children of the faithful. For although Solomon had infused knowledge of natural things, and of many supernatural and mystical things, yet he did not have it of all such hidden judgements of God: to search into these immoderately is reckoned curious and rash, since it wholly exceeds the capacity of human weakness. Therefore of such things we must say with the Apostle: [[Rom 11:33|O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!|O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, et investigabiles viæ ejus!]] and with the Psalmist: [[Ps 35:7|thy judgments are a great deep|Judicia tua abyssus multa]].

paras.t: Hanc occupationem pessimam, id est curiosam investigationem, et immoderatam inquisitionem de omnibus quæ fiunt sub cœlo, dedit Deus filiis hominum, id est, permisit eos ipsam assumere. Juxta quem modum ait Apostolus: Mittet illis Deus operationem erroris, ut credant mendacio: et rursus, Tradidit illos Deus in passiones ignominiæ. Sic quoque Isaias loquitur Deo: Quare nos errare fecisti de viis tuis, indurasti corda nostra ne timeremus te? Ut occuparentur in ea, neglectis his quæ pertinent ad salutem. Et certe nunc usque videmus quam vere sit ita, qualiter multi quæstiones sine numero multiplicent, et vanissimis sophistriis ac curiositatibus sint intenti, omissa divinorum observantia præceptorum. In qua occupatione stultissima multi quoque religiosi sic involvuntur, quod observantias negligunt regulares. Qui utinam illud Ecclesiastici rite adverterent : Altiora te ne quæsieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris; sed quæ præcepit tibi Deus, illa cogita semper, et in pluribus operibus ejus ne fueris curiosus. Non est enim tibi necessarium, ea quæ abscondita sunt, videre oculis tuis. Unde et Apostolus Timotheum discipulum monens : Stultas, inquit, et sine disciplina quæstiones devita, sciens quia generant lites.
paras.en: [[1:13|This painful occupation|Hanc occupationem pessimam]] [Denis's Latin, pessimam, is literally "most evil"], that is, curious investigation and immoderate inquiry into all things that are done under heaven, [[1:13|hath God given to the children of men|dedit Deus filiis hominum]], that is, he permitted them to take it up. In the same manner the Apostle says: [[2 Thess 2:10|God shall send them the operation of error, to believe lying|Mittet illis Deus operationem erroris, ut credant mendacio]]; and again: [[Rom 1:26|God delivered them up to shameful affections|Tradidit illos Deus in passiones ignominiæ]]. So too Isaias says to God: [[Is 63:17|Why hast thou made us to err|Quare nos errare fecisti]], [[Is 63:17|from thy ways: why hast thou hardened our heart, that we should not fear thee?|de viis tuis, indurasti corda nostra ne timeremus te?]] [[1:13|to be exercised therein|Ut occuparentur in ea]], neglecting the things that belong to salvation. And indeed down to this day we see how truly it is so: how many multiply questions without number, and are intent on the vainest sophistries and curiosities, leaving aside the keeping of the divine commandments. In this most foolish occupation many religious too are so entangled that they neglect the observances of their rule. Would that they rightly heeded that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:22|Seek not the things that are too high for thee, and search not into things above thy ability: but the things that God hath commanded thee, think on them always, and in many of his works be not curious|Altiora te ne quæsieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris; sed quæ præcepit tibi Deus, illa cogita semper, et in pluribus operibus ejus ne fueris curiosus]]. [[Ecclus 3:23|For it is not necessary for thee to see with thy eyes those things that are hid|Non est enim tibi necessarium, ea quæ abscondita sunt, videre oculis tuis]]. Hence the Apostle too, warning his disciple Timothy: [[2 Tim 2:23|avoid foolish|Stultas]], he says, [[2 Tim 2:23|and unlearned questions, knowing that they beget strifes|et sine disciplina quæstiones devita, sciens quia generant lites]].

paras.t: Vidi cuncta quæ fiunt sub sole, id est, consideravi ea, saltem in generali, et multa in speciali; vel, Cuncta, id est quædam de omnibus illis, ut sit distributio pro generibus singulorum : juxta quem sensum ait Psalmista Deo, Narrabo omnia mirabilia tua. Et ecce universa vanitas, et afflictio spiritus : id est, vanitas omnibus illis fuit admixta, vanumque fuit, laboriosum, et animæ afflictivum, considerationi et perscrutationi omnium illorum insistere. Imo occupatio talis impedit hominem ab utilioribus et salubrioribus actibus, ab exercitio orationis et devotionis, ab inflammatione affectus, ab expurgatione discussioneque mentis : quia quo mens circa plura distenditur atque dispergitur, eo minus circa unum illud quod summe necessarium est, recolligitur et constabilitur. Hinc Apostolus hortatur nos, ut quæramus meliora et viciniora saluti. Et rursus : Doctrinis, inquit, variis et peregrinis nolite abduci. Optimum enim est gratia stabilire cor.
paras.en: [[1:14|I have seen all things that are done under the sun|Vidi cuncta quæ fiunt sub sole]], that is, I have considered them, at least in general, and many of them in particular; or, "all things", that is, some of all those things, so that the word is taken of every kind of thing, not of every single thing [a scholastic distinction: distributio pro generibus singulorum, "all" meaning some of each kind, not each one]: in which sense the Psalmist says to God: [[Ps 9:2|I will relate all thy wonders|Narrabo omnia mirabilia tua]]. [[1:14|and behold all is vanity, and vexation of spirit|Et ecce universa vanitas, et afflictio spiritus]]: that is, vanity was mixed in with all those things, and it was vain, laborious and afflicting to the soul to give oneself to the consideration and searching out of all of them. Indeed such an occupation hinders a man from more useful and wholesome acts: from the exercise of prayer and devotion, from the kindling of the affections, from the cleansing and examining of the mind; for the more the mind is stretched out and scattered over many things, the less it is gathered and settled upon that one thing which is supremely necessary. Hence the Apostle exhorts us to seek [[Heb 6:9|better things|meliora]], [[Heb 6:9|and nearer to salvation|et viciniora saluti]]. And again he says: [[Heb 13:9|Be not led away with various and strange doctrines|variis et peregrinis nolite abduci]]. [[Heb 13:9|For it is best that the heart be established with grace|Optimum enim est gratia stabilire cor]].

paras.t: Perversi difficile corriguntur : quia sunt habituati in vitiis. Difficile autem est consueta relinquere. Imo, secundum Philosophum, tales dicuntur incurabiles. Verumtamen per auxilium et miserationem Spiritus Sancti possunt converti. Et stultorum infinitus est numerus. Omnis numerus est finitus, quum numerus sit certa et determinata mensura, seu computatio rerum numeratarum. Quomodo ergo stultorum infinitus est numerus ? Respondendum, quod cuncta creata, finita sunt, absolute loquendo, utpote in numero, pondere, et mensura constituta. Sed quantum ad nos multitudo stultorum est infinita, quia innumerabilis nobis est, nec numerum eorum habemus; sed Deus eorum numerum novit. Stulti autem, in Scripturis vocantur, universi qui dono sapientiæ carent, omnes videlicet qui in mortali sunt culpa : quia in illis puerilitatis vitium seu insipientia regnat (quoniam summo, infinito et invariabili bono præferunt vana, carnalia et caduca); sicut pueri poma et pira auro et gemmis præponunt, sic ipsi sensibilia et terrena, spiritualibus et divinis. Sed quum Psalmista de electis et sapientibus dicat, Dinumerabo eos, et super arenam multiplicabuntur; videtur quod sapientium quoque infinitus sit numerus. Respondetur, quod utique innumerabilis nobis est multitudo justorum, sapientium et electorum; nihilo minus multitudo reproborum ac impiorum multo innumerabilior est : quia in tantum est major, ut dicat Salvator, Multi sunt vocati, pauci vero electi.
paras.en: [[1:15|The perverse are hard to be corrected|Perversi difficile corriguntur]]: because they are habituated in vices, and it is hard to give up what one is used to. Indeed, according to the Philosopher, such men are called incurable. Yet by the help and mercy of the Holy Ghost they can be converted. [[1:15|and the number of fools is infinite|Et stultorum infinitus est numerus]]. Every number is finite, since number is a certain and determinate measure, or count, of the things numbered. How then is the number of fools infinite? The answer is that all created things are finite, speaking absolutely, being established in number, weight and measure[[Wis 11:21||]]. But as far as we are concerned the multitude of fools is infinite, because it is innumerable to us, and we do not have their number; but God knows their number. Now in the Scriptures all those are called fools who lack the gift of wisdom, namely all who are in mortal sin: because in them reigns the vice of childishness, or folly (since they prefer vain, carnal and perishable things to the highest, infinite and unchangeable good); as children prefer apples and pears to gold and gems, so they prefer things of sense and of earth to things spiritual and divine. But since the Psalmist says of the elect and the wise: [[Ps 138:18|I will number them, and they shall be multiplied above the sand|Dinumerabo eos, et super arenam multiplicabuntur]], it seems that the number of the wise too is infinite. The answer is that the multitude of the just, the wise and the elect is indeed innumerable to us; nevertheless the multitude of the reprobate and the wicked is far more innumerable: for it is so much greater that the Saviour says: [[Matt 20:16|many are called but few chosen|Multi sunt vocati, pauci vero electi]][[Matt 22:14||]].

paras.t: Locutus sum in corde meo, id est, cogitavi, dicens intra me, vel etiam aliis : Ecce magnus effectus sum. Salomon enim fuit rex valde magnus, famosus, potens, opulentus, et præsertim in sapientia, eminens aliis. Ideo subditur, et præcessi omnes sapientia, qui fuerunt ante me in Jerusalem. Imo in toto mundo non erat tempore suo æqualis ei in sapientia atque scientia, prout tertio Regum et secundo Paralipomenon satis ostenditur. Quod qualiter intelligendum sit, tertio Regum diligenter expositum est. Non enim potest illud intelligi de sapientia, ut est donum : quia illa est tanto major in homine, quanto perfectior ipse est in caritate. Ideo, sicut David fuit sanctior Salomone, ita et sapientior eo fuit, loquendo de sapientia quæ est unum de septem donis. Loquendo autem de sapientia et scientia, ut sunt dona gratiæ gratis datæ, et de cognitione naturalium rerum, Salomon sapientissimus fuit in populo. Potuit quoque istam suam excellentiam sine peccato attendere ac fateri, dummodo eam Deo attribuit, quoniam ex revelatione divina scivit se eam habere. Sic namque et David grata ac humili mente dixit ad Dominum : Fecisti me spectabilem præ omnibus hominibus. Apostolus quoque : Nos ipsi, inquit, primitias Spiritus habentes.
paras.en: [[1:16|I have spoken in my heart|Locutus sum in corde meo]], that is, I thought, saying within myself, or even to others: [[1:16|Behold I am become great|Ecce magnus effectus sum]]. For Solomon was a very great king, famous, mighty, wealthy, and above all eminent over others in wisdom. Therefore it is added: [[1:16|and have gone beyond all in wisdom, that were before me in Jerusalem|et præcessi omnes sapientia, qui fuerunt ante me in Jerusalem]]. Indeed in the whole world there was no one in his time equal to him in wisdom and knowledge, as is amply shown in the third book of Kings and the second of Paralipomenon[[3 Kings 3:12||]][[3 Kings 4:29||]][[3 Kings 10:7||]][[2 Par 1:12||]][[2 Par 9:6||]] [the margin gives 3 Kings 4:29–34 for the second of these]. How this is to be understood has been carefully explained on the third book of Kings. For it cannot be understood of wisdom as it is a gift: for that is the greater in a man the more perfect he is in charity. Therefore, as David was holier than Solomon, so he was also wiser than he, speaking of the wisdom which is one of the seven gifts[[Is 11:2||]]. But speaking of wisdom and knowledge as they are gifts of grace freely given [gratia gratis data: graces given chiefly for the good of others, such as prophecy, as distinct from the grace that makes a man holy], and of the knowledge of natural things, Solomon was the wisest among the people. He could also attend to this excellence of his and acknowledge it without sin, so long as he attributed it to God, since he knew by divine revelation that he had it. For so David too, with a grateful and humble mind, said to the Lord: Thou [[1 Par 17:17|hast made me remarkable above all men|Fecisti me spectabilem præ omnibus hominibus]].
